transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: alright everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus today's sesh on the raw runtime profiles we ran — TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, and talk through kernel selection and cuda graphs. hi all?
[00:10] Priya Mehta: hey Samir, yeah excited — we've been seeing variance in tail latency when context >8k so hoping to see root causes.
[00:22] Lena Cho: quick note — some of the term's in the runs got munged, so you'll see "Tensorrt-llm" or "v l l m" in the trace labels, that's from the collector.
[00:35] Carlos Ruiz: cc: we've got the staging nodes up — A100 80GB, NCCL / on-prem networking is 100g.
[00:42] Tom Anders: one ask, priya asked to focus on KV cache warm vs cold numbers, because our workload does long chats and alot of re-reads.
[00:50] Samir Patel: perfect, lena can you walk through the TensorRT-LLM run?
[01:03] Lena Cho: yeah so first slide, baseline: single-stream, 1 token step latency and throughput numbers, we then scaled to batch sizes 1/4/8/16 and seq lens 2k/8k/16k. Observed that TensorRT-LLM selected fused attention kernels for 4k-ish heads/seq, but when sequence grew to 16k it fell back to chunked kernels — that's where we saw kernel-selection overhead.
[01:30] Priya Mehta: chunked kernels meaning?
[01:36] Lena Cho: so there's a handoff — the runtime chooses a different CUDA kernel variant optimized for long sequences; those have more shared memory and register pressure, so they show higher per-token latency but better memory utilization. On our traces you'll see that as a switch from kernel name like "attn_fused_v2" to "attn_chunked_v1" and accompanying cuda graph replay overhead.
[02:01] Carlos Ruiz: interesting, we noticed more host-device syncs in some runs, could that be graph replay syncing?
[02:08] Miguel Torres: yes, we instrumented CUDA graph capture/launch; when graphs were re-captured mid-run due to kernel fallback it adds 10-30ms spikes. Also if the KV cache size changes it invalidates captures.
[02:25] Tom Anders: vLLM side?
[02:28] Lena Cho: vLLM uses a different scheduling: micro-batching with aggressive KV cache reuse; it avoids some graph recaptures but it relies on custom optimized kernels (less fused) so per-token throughput varies. In our benchmark vLLM had slightly lower median latency for 2k-8k but when you go to 16k TensorRT edges out in throughput after warmup — but cost was higher per GPU-hour.
[02:55] Priya Mehta: we care about tail more than median. What about 99th percentile?
[03:00] Lena Cho: great question — 99th in TensorRT runs spiked when graphs recaptured, also when kernel selection path triggered different memory alloc pattern. We added small jitter in request size to force more stable captures; that helped but not perfect.
[03:20] Samir Patel: on KV cache — did you profile warm vs cold?
[03:24] Miguel Torres: yes, warm KV cache reduced token gen time by ~18-23% median. But note that large KV caches cause memory pressure and can push kernel variant selection into chunked paths.
[03:40] Dana Li: on our infra the SREs saw occasional OOMs when batch sizes >8 for 16k seqs, is that from chunked kernels or memory accounting mismatch?
[03:49] Lena Cho: more likely memory accounting + allocation fragmentation; TensorRT's allocator behaves slightly different versus PyTorch allocator used by vLLM. We recommend pre-reserving large buffers and using a predictable allocation policy for on-prem.
[04:05] Priya Mehta: how about quantization? we've been evaluating 4-bit QAT and post-training quant, any gotchas?
[04:12] Lena Cho: quant is great for throughput but watch accuracy/regression. For runtime, int4 kernels sometimes cause kernel fallback to slower verification paths when values saturate; also certain fused kernels don't have int4 implementations so you drop to slower path. We saw a 10% latency regression on some endpoints after naive quant.
[04:35] Tom Anders: so tradeoff is cost vs quality vs tail?
[04:38] Samir Patel: yes. Another item — batching strategy: continuous batching in our runtime allows combining small requests with similar sequence patterns; vLLM's microbatching is effective for small tokens but TensorRT found better scaling when batches are aggregated by target length.
[04:55] Carlos Ruiz: networking — VPC peering and on-prem: any gotchas for us?
[05:00] Lena Cho: if you're using dedicated on-prem with a private control plane, watch WAN latency for arg exchange and for KMS calls during inference (if you call KMS per-request for keys it adds latency). We saw KMS cold auth add ~120ms per call. For on-prem we recommend caching KMS tokens and local HSM gateways.
[05:22] Priya Mehta: thanks. can you show kernel flamegraphs?
[05:25] Lena Cho: sure uploading Nsight captures now — link in chat.
[05:32] [screen share starts]
[05:40] Lena Cho: here's a TensorRT run flamegraph — you can see big blocks for fused matmul+softmax, then smaller blocks where CUDA graph capture + replay occurs. There's a visible spike where kernel variant switches mid-sequence.
[06:05] Tom Anders: in the vLLM profile we see a lot of small kernels — is that overhead from micro batch scheduling?
[06:11] Miguel Torres: yep, more kernels = more launch overhead but lower per-kernel memory pressure. Net effect depends on your lat distribution.
[06:30] Priya Mehta: if we had to pick a config for low tail latency at 8k context which would you recommend?
[06:36] Lena Cho: for low tail I'd recommend vLLM with warm KV cache + reserved buffers and small microbatching, or TensorRT with pre-captured cuda graphs for the common sequence lengths and aggressive buffer reservation. There's a tradeoff: TensorRT with graphs gives best throughput & lower median after warmup but needs careful capture management to keep tail down.
[06:58] Carlos Ruiz: any automated tooling to detect when graphs need re-capture?
[07:03] Lena Cho: yes, our runtime emits graph invalidation events and a heuristics engine that triggers re-capture during low-traffic windows. We're improving heuristics to avoid doing it mid-stream.
[07:15] Samir Patel: note on kernel selection visibility — we can export kernel mapping for each trace so you can correlate 99th spikes to kernel variant. Lena will include that.
[07:29] Priya Mehta: sounds good. about quantization: can we stage it only on non-critical routes?
[07:34] Samir Patel: absolutely canary quantized variants with rollouts and automatic fallback if quality regressions detected by evals.
[07:40] Tom Anders: we saw in one run that host-device syncs came from logging hooks, any recs?
[07:45] Miguel Torres: avoid synchronous logging in the hot loop; use async buffers and batch flushes. Also watch for debug builds with extra syncs.
[07:56] Priya Mehta: on security, we need SOC2 audit docs and HSM/KMS integration details for Private.
[08:03] Samir Patel: will share SOC2 artifact and KMS integration guide after this call.
[08:09] Carlos Ruiz: for the POC, we'll want to run both TensorRT and vLLM stacks on our on-prem A100s, compare 8k/16k, and measure 95/99/median and cost per token.
[08:20] Lena Cho: agreed — we'll produce cost model estimates factoring reserved capacity and warmup profiles.
[08:27] [15:00] --- (middle of call, lots of profiling detail, omitted long table paste) ---
[23:10] Lena Cho: we had one anomaly — an allocation pattern in the cuda graph replay loop causing fragmentation, fixed it by switching to a pooled allocator which reduced 99th by 18%.
[27:45] Tom Anders: can you remind us about KV eviction policy options?
[27:51] Lena Cho: LRU vs size-based TTL — for chat style with repeated references LRU is best; for long single-session transcripts size-based eviction prevents old sessions from monopolizing memory. We'll include recommended settings.
[34:10] Miguel Torres: also note when using quantized KV the memory drop is significant but CPU dequant cost appears in some kernels, so verify kernel-level support.
[40:00] Priya Mehta: okay i think we have enough to run the POC. Heads-up: procurement might ask about enterprise licensing for Private deploys.
[40:10] Samir Patel: understood, we'll include pricing ranges and reserved capacity options in follow-up.
[41:05] Carlos Ruiz: one more: are there recommended batch-size caps for 16k seqs on A100 80GB to avoid OOM?
[41:12] Lena Cho: recommend batch <=8 with pre-reserved buffers for 16k; for >8 use model parallel or sequence sharding. We'll document exact memory numbers per model archetype.
[50:00] Priya Mehta: thanks everyone — recap next steps?
[50:05] Samir Patel: recap: share traces + spreadsheet, run 8k/16k extra profiles, provide SOC2 & KMS docs, schedule POC kickoff.
[50:18] Tom Anders: i'll follow up on scheduling and share internal stakeholder list.
[50:25] [end 62:00]
